newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: SOUTH AUSTRALIAN FIRM FINED FOR WINE SUBSTITUTION
A Federal Court judge has fined a South Australian company found guilty of wine substitution, saying that such fraud could seriously damage the wine industry.
Justice O'Loughlin has fined bulk wine supplier, Vales Wine Company, now in liquidation, a total of 165-thousand dollars.
The company and its directors had been found guilty of selling almost 200-thousand litres of wine in 1991, falsely described as McLaren Vale cabernet sauvignon.
Justice O'Loughlin has fined former directors, Michael Baron Von Berg and Claude Curtis, 10-thousand dollars each, saying that both men's conduct was deliberate.
He says the wine industry depends on the integrity of winemakers and manufacturers.
A$4.4 MILLION PAYOUT OVER NSW CAR ACCIDENT
A woman has won A$4.4 million dollars in damages over an
accident in which her car crashed on a newly resurfaced road in New South Wales' Hunter region two and a half years ago.
Sydney judge, Peter McInerney, says Dungog Shire Council and Boral Asphalt failed to remove excess stone from the road surface, and failed in their duty of care to motorists on the road.
The Judge says Philippa McKenny has been reduced to a life of extreme disability with all the frustrations that entails.
He says he intends awarding the damages to cover her medical expenses and lost income.
The Defendants are considering appealing.
PAYOUT ORDERED OVER AIRBAG MISHAP
American car manufacturer, the Chrysler Corporation, has been ordered to pay nearly US$50,000 to a woman who was injured when an airbag inflated during a minor traffic accident.
The jury found Chrysler liable for the fractured elbow Mary Bresnahan suffered in the 1990 accident, as the airbag had pushed her arm into the windscreen frame.
Ms Bresnahan has had four operations on her elbow since then.
The woman's lawyer says the ruling marks the first time a car-maker has been held liable for injuries caused by an airbag.
Lawyers for Chrysler say the company will appeal.
PREMIERS WANT MORE FUNDING FOR GUN BUYBACK
The fragile national gun buyback scheme has hit more trouble with State Premiers saying the Commonwealth hasn't given them enough money to run the operation.
Queensland says it won't bring in uniform national gun laws unless the Commonwealth makes up a shortfall of about eight million dollars in funding for administering the state's gun buyback scheme.

And New South Wales Police Minister, Paul Whelan, says he'll have to find his state's A$4 million dollar shortfall from the police budget, if the Commonwealth doesn't come up with more than the 66 cents in the dollar promised.
Premiers will ask the Prime Minister to reconsider the level of funding for the gun buyback, at Friday's meeting of premiers and chief ministers.
MINISTER ADMITS STRIKES WILL INCREASE
Federal Industrial Relations Minister, Peter Reith, concedes there will be a rise in industrial action associated with the Government's industrial reforms.
The Government this week reopened negotiations with the Senate minor parties over its Work Place Relations Bill, due to be debated in Parliament early next month.
Mr Reith says the industrial action is being conducted by unions who object to what he describes as sensible changes.
However, he predicts industrial harmony will return once the reforms, including a greater emphasis on enterprise bargaining, take effect.
NO MORE AFL GRAND FINAL TICKETS ISSUED
The AFL won't be allocating any more tickets to Swans members wanting to see their team play in the Grand Final on Saturday.
Hundreds of Sydney supporters missed out on tickets for the match, when the 7,500 made available to the club, sold out.
Swans officials are furious many members won't be able to see the premiership match against North Melbourne.
And Sydney has another worry, with an incident involving Andrew Dunkley and Bomber, James Hird, being investigated.
Hird left the field with blood streaming down his face, and needed stiches.
The result of the probe should be known later today.
AUSTUDY TIGHTENING DEFENDED
A Government Senator says there's clear evidence to justify the Coalition's tighter eligibility test for Austudy, with about 5-thousand millionaire families paid Austudy and other welfare benefits.

Senator Jeannie Ferris says a Senate inquiry has heard the families had been able to claim a taxable income as low as six thousand dollars, and access Austudy and other Commonwealth benefits worth more than 20-thousand dollars.
Senator Ferris says the Department of Employment, Education, Training and Youth Affairs estimates about two percent of Austudy recipients had been rorting the system.
She says 10,500 families had Austudy payments
withdrawn as a result of the Department's inquiry and imposing the new elgibility test.
RIDGE ADVISED NOT TO PLAY BY NEURO SURGEON
An Auckland neuro-surgeon has warned Manly fullback Matthew Ridge that he risks incurring a fatal injury if he plays in Sunday's rugby league grand final in Sydney.
Ridge, who's also captain of the New Zealand rugby league team was knocked unconscious in Manly's 24-nil semi-final win over Cronulla last Sunday, and was carried from the field.
He spent the night in North Shore Hospital, where he had a brain scan before being released the following day.
Manly coach Bob Fulton has insisted Ridge will play in the final against St George, but Dr Philip Wrightson says there's a small risk of a fatal reaction, if he's knocked out again a week later.
Dr Wrightson says he'd also like to encourage rugby league
officials to follow rugby union's example in setting a mandatory three-week stand-down period for players who suffer concussion.
PNG WANTS POLYNESIA DECOLONISED
Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister, Sir Julius Chan, has suggested at the United Nations that French Polynesia be included in a list of countries to be decolonised.
The list is set up by the world body's De-colonisation Committee.
French Polynesia, which includes Tahiti, and the small islands of Wallis and Futuna, are French Overseas Territories, a status which gives them a large degree of autonomy.
Until January, France carried out a series of nuclear tests on Mururoa and Fangataufa, two islands in French Polynesia, despite widespread protests, particularly from the Asia-Pacific region.
France's envoy has dismissed Sir Julius' suggestion, saying the people of French Polynesia still believe that they're part of the French republic.
GOVERNMENT REJECTS GUN SCHEME CRITICISM
The Federal Government has again rejected claims that it's
short-changing the States over the guns buy-back scheme.
New South Wales and Queensland have criticised the Federal
Government's contribution and Queensland says it won't bring in uniform national gun laws unless the Commonwealth makes up a shortfall of about eight million dollars.
A spokesman for Federal Attorney-General, Daryl Williams, says the Government's been generous in agreeing to provide two-thirds of the cost of the scheme.
She says Mr Williams and Prime Minister, John Howard, believe the States should contribute to some extent.
She says the Commonwealth is paying its fair share of the public education campaign and hopes the States will continue to negotiate and abide by the buy-back agreement reached in May.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
